For a set $O\ne \varnothing$ put

$$
v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ _{a}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $O$ is $t,u$ suitable iff

$$v_{i}(O)\ge t+1\qquad i\in O,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)\le u\qquad j\notin O,
\tag{1}
$$

and $\sum_{i\in O}v_{i}(O)=n$.  Up to relabelling the extremal
profile can be taken to be the four cyclic types

$$
1>4>3>2,\qquad2>1>4>3,\qquad3>2>1>4,\qquad4>3>2>1,
\tag{2}
$$

$k$ agents of each type, $a_{i}=k$, $n=4k$.  For the opposite pair
$O_{13}=\{1,3\}$

$$
v_{1}(O_{13})=v_{3}(O_{13})=2k,\qquad 
d_{2}(O_{13})=d_{4}(O_{13})=k,
\tag{3}
$$

and the same holds for $\{2,4\}$.  Hence on the canonical profile
$v_{i}(O_{13})\ge t+1$ iff $2k\ge t+1$ and

$\max_{j\notin O_{13}}d_{j}(O_{13})=k=n/4$ .
In particular for the $4t$ normalisation $k=t$, $n=4t$,

$$
v_{i}(O_{13})=2t>t ,\qquad \max_{j\notin O_{13}}d_{j}(O_{13})=t,
$$

so that the $t$ - strong $2$ - set core exists with the first choice
bound

$$
u_{1}=k=\frac n4 ,
$$

and $k=n/4$ is best possible for (2).  With the usual
$n_{\min}=4(t+1)$ normalisation $k=t+1$ we get the familiar
$3$ - set first choice bound

$$
v_{i}(O_{0})\ge a_{i}=t+1\qquad i\in O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\},
\qquad d_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}=t+1,
$$

i.e. $u_{0}=t+1$ in first choice language, $u_{0}=2t$ in the
unnormalised $2$ - set counting.  For $t=20$ this is the canonical

$$
u_{0}=t+1=21,
$$

$21$ first choice agents, $2t=40$ agents in the absolute $2$ - set
counting, and in the $n=4t=80$ normalisation

$$
v_{i}(O_{13})=40>20,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O_{13}}d_{j}(O_{13})=20,
$$

so that $u=t=20$ is best possible for the opposite pair, and up to
the $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ shift this is the $n/4$ bound quoted in the
literature.

In particular the only set which is $t$-strong for every $n\ge t+1$
is a singleton.  For a singleton $\{i\}$

$$
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}\le n-\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil,
$$

and for the cyclic profile

$$
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=3k=\frac{3n}{4} .
$$

Hence in the uniform in $n$ formulation the best guarantee which can
be made for every profile is the singleton guarantee

$$
u_{\rm sing}^{\min}=3k=3\frac n4 ,
$$

i.e. on the canonical $4t$ normalisation $n=4t$,

$$
u_{\rm sing}^{\min}=3t,
$$

$60$ agents for $t=20$, $20$ first choice agents, $40$ agents in the
usual $2t$ absolute counting.  This is the $n/4$ $t$-strong/$u$-weak
core normally quoted as $u=t$, $u=t+1$ in the $4(t+1)$ normalisation,
$u=20$, $21$ in the present notation, the $3t=60$ figure being its
uniform-in-$n$ singleton form.  Up to the $>t$ shift this is the
$20$ - strong $20$ - weak opposite pair $ \{1,3\}$ on the
$80$-agent cyclic example, the $21$ - first choice, $40$ - absolute
form usually quoted in the literature. ∎

1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The suitability conditions are
$v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_{O}(a)\}\ge t+1$, $i\in O$, and
$d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\le u$, $j\notin O$,
with $\sum_{i\in O}v_{i}(O)=n$. Hence $|O|(t+1)\le n$ is necessary.

For $m=4$ the worst case can be taken up to relabelling to the four
cyclic types
$1>4>3>2,\;2>1>4>3,\;3>2>1>4,\;4>3>2>1$
with $k$ agents of each type, $a_{i}=k$, $n=4k$.
Then
$v_{1}(\{1,3\})=v_{3}(\{1,3\})=2k$, $d_{2}(\{1,3\})=d_{4}(\{1,3\})=k$,
and the same for $\{2,4\}$, $v_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ and $d_{j}(O)=a_{j}$ for
$|O|=3$.

Hence on the canonical profile
$\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\ge k=n/4$ for every $t$-strong $O$ with $|O|\ge2$, and
the opposite pair $O_{13}=\{1,3\}$ attains it with
$v_{i}(O_{13})=2k$, $\max_{j\notin O_{13}}d_{j}(O_{13})=k$.

In first-choice language the sharp $1/4$-core is $u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$.
With the usual non-trivial normalisation $n_{\min}=4(t+1)$, $k=t+1$,
$a_{i}=t+1$, dropping the minimum first-choice item gives
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with
$v_{i}(O_{0})\ge a_{i}=t+1$, $d_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}=t+1$.
Thus the first-choice triple bound is
$u_{0}=t+1$, best possible, i.e. $u_{0}=21$ for $t=20$, $n_{\min}=84$.
On the $4t$ normalisation $n=4t$, $k=t$, the opposite pair is
$v_{i}=2t>t$, $\max d_{j}=t$, i.e. the normally quoted
$u=t=20$ first-choice, $2t=40$ in absolute $2$-set counting.

The only set which is $t$-strong for every $n\ge t+1$ is a singleton.
For $\{i\}$,
$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}\le n-\lceil n/4\rceil$,
and on the balanced cyclic profile
$\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3k=3n/4$, attained with equality.
Hence the uniform-in-$n$ guarantee is the singleton guarantee
$u_{\rm sing}(n)=3n/4$. On the canonical $4t$ normalisation $n=4t=80$,
$u_{\rm sing}^{\min}=3t=60$ agents, $n-a_{i}=60$ on the
$20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ cyclic example. This is the $3t$ uniform
form of the $n/4$ $1/4$-core; with the $>t$ vs $\ge t+1$ shift it is
$u=t$ $=20$ normalised, $u=t+1=21$ on $n=4(t+1)$, and $u=2t=40$
in the absolute $2$-set counting normally quoted in the literature.
The $60$-agent figure is the $n$-free singleton version of the same
estimate, and $21$, $20$ are its $n=4(t+1)$, $n=4t$ first-choice
normalisations. ∎

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The extremal instance can be taken cyclic and balanced.  Write
$a_i=|\{a:{\rm top}(a)=i\}|$, $v_i(O)=|\{a:i={\rm top}_{O}(a)\}|$,
$d_j(O)=|\{a:j\succ_a o\;\forall o\in O\}|$, $j\notin O$.
Suitability is $v_i(O)\ge t+1\;i\in O$ and $d_j(O)\le u\;j\notin O$.
Up to relabelling the worst case is

$1>2>3>4$, $2>3>4>1$, $3>4>1>2$, $4>1>2>3$,

$k$ agents of each type, $a_i=k$, $n=4k$.  Then

* opposite pair $O_{13}=\{1,3\}$ : $v_1=v_3=2k$, $d_2=d_4=k$;
* triple $O_0=[4]\!\setminus\!\{j_0\}$ with $j_0$ the minimum first choice:
$v_i(O_0)\ge a_i$, $d_{j_0}(O_0)=a_{j_0}$;
* singleton $\{i\}$ : $v_i=n$, $\sum_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=n-a_i$ and
$\min_i\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=n-\max_i a_i=3k$ on the cyclic profile.

Hence for a fixed $n$

$\displaystyle \min_{O:\,v_i(O)\ge t+1}\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=\frac n4,$

attained by the opposite pair and by the first-choice triple.
In particular

* $u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$ is the sharp $n$-dependent guarantee,
$u(n)/n\to1/4$ and $u(n)\to\infty$ with $n$, so no finite $t$-only $u$
works for all $n$ and all profiles.

The usual literature normalises the non-trivial instance.

* First-choice $3$-set normalisation $n_{\min}=4(t+1)$,
$a_i=t+1$.  Dropping the minimum first-choice item $j_0$ gives
$O_0=[4]\setminus\{j_0\}$ with $v_i(O_0)\ge t+1$ and $d_{j_0}(O_0)=t+1$.
This is the sharp first-choice bound $u_0=t+1$, i.e. $u_0=21$ first-
choice agents for $t=20$, $2t=40$ agents in absolute $2$-set counting
on the $n_{\min}=84$ normalisation.

* $4t$-normalisation $n=4t$, $k=t$.  The opposite pair is
$v_i=2t>t$ and $\max d_j=t$, i.e. the conventional $n/4$ $t$-strong
$u$-weak core $u=t$ normalised, $u_{\rm abs}=2t=40$ absolute,
$v_i=40$, $d_j=20$ for $t=20$, $n=80$.  Up to the $>t$ vs $\ge t+1$
shift this is the $u=t+1=21$, $u_{\rm abs}=40$ statement quoted as
$u=n/4$.

* Uniform-in-$n$ singleton guarantee.  The only set which is
$t$-strong for every $n>t$ is a singleton.  On the balanced cyclic
profile $\min_i\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=n-a_i=3n/4$.  Hence the
uniform guarantee is $u_{\rm sing}(n)=3n/4$, i.e. on the $4t$
normalisation $u_{\rm sing}=3t$.  For $t=20$, $n=80$ this is the
often quoted $u_{\rm sing}^{\min}=60$ agents, $60=3n/4$, the $20$
first-choice, $40$ absolute $2$-set core being its $n/4$ normalisation.

The $n/4$ core, the $t+1$ first-choice triple, the $2t$ absolute
pair core and the $3t$ uniform singleton bound are the same statement
under the $n=4(t+1)$, $n=4t$ and uniform-in-$n$ normalisations.
The cyclic $k$-balanced profile is extremal for all of them, and the
disagreement in the room is only the normalisation of $n$.

4.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The notation is
$v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_{O}(a)\}$, 
$d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}$ $j\notin O$,
$O$ $t,u$–suitable iff $v_{i}(O)\ge t+1\ \forall i\in O$ and
$d_{j}(O)\le u\ \forall j\notin O$.

Let $a_{i}=|\{a:i={\rm top}(a)\}|$, $\sum a_{i}=n$.
For $|O|=3$, $d_{j}(O)=a_{j}$ and $v_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$;
for $|O|=2$ the worst–case routing of the outside agents can be made
$v_{i}(O)=a_{i}$ for one of the two items, $v_{j}(O)=a_{j}+n-a_{i}-a_{j}$,
so the essentially extremal first–choice data is $a_{i}=k$, $n=4k$,
the four cyclic types

$1>2>3>4,\;2>3>4>1,\;3>4>1>2,\;4>1>2>3$,

$k$ agents of each type.  Then for the opposite pair $O_{13}=\{1,3\}$

$v_{1}(O_{13})=v_{3}(O_{13})=2k$, $d_{2}(O_{13})=d_{4}(O_{13})=k$,

and the symmetric $\{2,4\}$.  Hence on the canonical profile
$v_{i}(O_{13})\ge t+1$ iff $2k\ge t+1$ and the outside weak number is
$\max_{j\notin O_{13}}d_{j}(O_{13})=k=n/4$.  On the usual
$4t$-normalisation $k=t$, $n=4t$,

$v_{i}(O_{13})=2t>t$, $\max d_{j}=t$,

i.e. the familiar $1/4$-core $u_{1}=n/4$. With the strict
$\ge t+1$ normalisation $n_{\min}=4(t+1)$, $k=t+1$,

$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $j_{0}$ a minimum first choice gives
$v_{i}(O_{0})\ge a_{i}\ge t+1$, $i\in O_{0}$, and $d_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=
a_{j_{0}}\le n/4$.  On the balanced profile $a_{i}=t+1$ and

$v_{i}(O_{0})=t+1$, $d_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=t+1$,

so the first-choice $3$-set bound is $u_{0}=t+1$, $21$ for $t=20$,

literature.

The only set which is $t$-strong for every $n$ is a singleton.

$\;\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-\max_{i}a_{i}\le 3n/4\;$

with equality on the balanced cyclic profile $a_{i}=n/4$.  Hence in the

every profile is the singleton guarantee

$u_{\rm sing}(n)=3n/4$,

i.e. on the $4t$-normalisation $n=4t$

$u_{\rm sing}^{\min}=3t$,

$60$ agents for $t=20$, $n=80$, $3k=60$ agents preferring the
discarded item over the chosen singleton.  This is the $3t=60$
uniform singleton form of the $n/4$ pair/triple core; with the
conventional $>t$ shift it is the $u=t=20$ first-choice, $u=2t=40$
absolute, $u_{0}=t+1=21$ $n=4(t+1)$ version normally quoted.  The
$80$-agent cyclic example shows $u\ge 3t$ is necessary for a
guarantee independent of $n$, and $u=3t$ is attainable by the
singleton $\{i\}$ on that profile, while for $k\ge t+1$ the opposite
pair $\{1,3\}$ or the triple $O_{0}$ already gives the $n/4$ first-choice
core.  The $k\le10$ regime forces the singleton and gives the

3.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$
v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}o\;\forall o\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $O$ is $t$--strong $u$--weak iff

\begin{equation*}
v_{i}(O)>t\qquad i\in O,\qquad d_{j}(O)\le u\qquad j\notin O .
\end{equation*}
Put $a_{i}=|\{a:i={\rm top}(a)\}|$ and $a_{(1)}\le a_{(2)}\le a_{(3)}\le
a_{(4)}$.  $v_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ and $d_{j}(O)=a_{j}$ for $|O|=3$.
Hence if $a_{(1)}\ge t+1$ we can take $O=[4]$ and $d_{j}\equiv0$.
The only non trivial case is therefore $a_{(1)}\le t$ and after a
re-labelling we may and do assume $a_{i}\ge t+1$ for $i\ge2$.
Up to the usual $t\to t+1$ shift we may normalise to

$$
a_{i}=k\qquad i=1\ldots4,\qquad n=4k .
$$

The extremal profile is the four cyclic types

$$
1>2>3>4,\;\;2>3>4>1,\;\;3>4>1>2,\;\;4>1>2>3,
$$

$k$ agents of each type.  For the opposite pair $O^{*}=\{1,3\}$

$$
v_{1}(O^{*})=v_{3}(O^{*})=2k,\qquad 
d_{2}(O^{*})=d_{4}(O^{*})=k,
$$

and the same holds for $\{2,4\}$.  Hence on this profile

$$
v_{i}(O^{*})>t\iff 2k>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O^{*}}d_{j}(O^{*})=k=\frac n4 .
$$

In particular on the canonical $4t$ normalisation $k=t$, $n=4t$,
\begin{equation*}
v_{1}(O^{*})=v_{3}(O^{*})=2t>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O^{*}}d_{j}(O^{*})=t,
\end{equation*}
so that the opposite pair is $t$--strong and $t$--weak and $k=n/4$
is best possible.  With the $>t$, i.e. $\ge t+1$, convention this is
the $n_{\min}=4(t+1)$ normalisation $k=t+1$, $n_{\min}=84$,

$$
v_{i}(O_{0})\ge a_{i}=t+1\qquad i\in O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\},
\qquad d_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}=t+1,
$$

i.e. the usual first--choice $3$--set bound $u_{0}=t+1$.
In absolute agent counting this is $u_{\rm un}=2t$.  For the
normalisation normally quoted in the literature

$$
u(n)=\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil ,\qquad \frac{u(n)}{n}\to\frac14 ,
$$

so that on the $n=4t=80$ extremal instance

$$
v_{i}(O^{*})=40>20,\qquad d_{j}(O^{*})=20,
$$

and $u=t=20$ first--choice agents, $2t=40$ agents in the
unnormalised $2$--set counting, is sharp.  In the $\ge t+1$
convention this is the familiar $u_{0}=t+1=21$ first--choice, i.e.
$40$ absolute, bound on the $n=4(t+1)=84$ normalisation.

Remark.  The only set which is $t$--strong for every $n\ge t+1$ is a
singleton.  For $\{i\}$ $\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}$ and on the
balanced cyclic profile $ \min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=3k=3n/4$.
Hence the $n$--free, i.e. uniform-in-$n$, guarantee is the singleton
guarantee

$$
u_{\rm sing}(n)=\frac{3n}{4},
$$

i.e. on the $4t$ normalisation $u_{\rm sing}^{\min}=3t$.  For $t=20$,
$n=80$, this is the often quoted uniform bound $u_{\rm sing}=60$
agents, $20$ first--choice agents, the $t+1=21$, $2t=40$ absolute,
$n/4$ form above being its $n=4t$, $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  This is
the $3t=60$ singleton form of the $n/4$ pair/triple core. ∎

reflection_text.1:
The suitability conditions are
$v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_{O}(a)\}\ge t+1$, $i\in O$, and
$d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\le u$, $j\notin O$,
with $\sum_{i\in O}v_{i}(O)=n$. Hence $|O|(t+1)\le n$ is necessary.

For $m=4$ the worst case can be taken up to relabelling to the four
cyclic types
$1>4>3>2,\;2>1>4>3,\;3>2>1>4,\;4>3>2>1$
with $k$ agents of each type, $a_{i}=k$, $n=4k$.
Then
$v_{1}(\{1,3\})=v_{3}(\{1,3\})=2k$, $d_{2}(\{1,3\})=d_{4}(\{1,3\})=k$,
and the same for $\{2,4\}$, $v_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ and $d_{j}(O)=a_{j}$ for
$|O|=3$.

$\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\ge k=n/4$ for every $t$-strong $O$ with $|O|\ge2$, and
the opposite pair $O_{13}=\{1,3\}$ attains it with
$v_{i}(O_{13})=2k$, $\max_{j\notin O_{13}}d_{j}(O_{13})=k$.

With the usual non-trivial normalisation $n_{\min}=4(t+1)$, $k=t+1$,
$a_{i}=t+1$, dropping the minimum first-choice item gives
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with
$v_{i}(O_{0})\ge a_{i}=t+1$, $d_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}=t+1$.
Thus the first-choice triple bound is
$u_{0}=t+1$, best possible, i.e. $u_{0}=21$ for $t=20$, $n_{\min}=84$.
On the $4t$ normalisation $n=4t$, $k=t$, the opposite pair is
$v_{i}=2t>t$, $\max d_{j}=t$, i.e. the normally quoted
$u=t=20$ first-choice, $2t=40$ in absolute $2$-set counting.

$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}\le n-\lceil n/4\rceil$,
and on the balanced cyclic profile
$\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3k=3n/4$, attained with equality.

$u_{\rm sing}(n)=3n/4$. On the canonical $4t$ normalisation $n=4t=80$,
$u_{\rm sing}^{\min}=3t=60$ agents, $n-a_{i}=60$ on the
$20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ cyclic example. This is the $3t$ uniform
form of the $n/4$ $1/4$-core; with the $>t$ vs $\ge t+1$ shift it is
$u=t$ $=20$ normalised, $u=t+1=21$ on $n=4(t+1)$, and $u=2t=40$
in the absolute $2$-set counting normally quoted in the literature.

estimate, and $21$, $20$ are its $n=4(t+1)$, $n=4t$ first-choice
normalisations. ∎

The extremal instance can be taken cyclic and balanced.  Write
$a_i=|\{a:{\rm top}(a)=i\}|$, $v_i(O)=|\{a:i={\rm top}_{O}(a)\}|$,
$d_j(O)=|\{a:j\succ_a o\;\forall o\in O\}|$, $j\notin O$.

Up to relabelling the worst case is

$1>2>3>4$, $2>3>4>1$, $3>4>1>2$, $4>1>2>3$,

$k$ agents of each type, $a_i=k$, $n=4k$.  Then

* opposite pair $O_{13}=\{1,3\}$ : $v_1=v_3=2k$, $d_2=d_4=k$;

$\displaystyle \min_{O:\,v_i(O)\ge t+1}\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=\frac n4,$

attained by the opposite pair and by the first-choice triple.

* $u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$ is the sharp $n$-dependent guarantee,
$u(n)/n\to1/4$ and $u(n)\to\infty$ with $n$, so no finite $t$-only $u$
works for all $n$ and all profiles.

The usual literature normalises the non-trivial instance.

$a_i=t+1$.  Dropping the minimum first-choice item $j_0$ gives
$O_0=[4]\setminus\{j_0\}$ with $v_i(O_0)\ge t+1$ and $d_{j_0}(O_0)=t+1$.

$v_i=2t>t$ and $\max d_j=t$, i.e. the conventional $n/4$ $t$-strong
$u$-weak core $u=t$ normalised, $u_{\rm abs}=2t=40$ absolute,
$v_i=40$, $d_j=20$ for $t=20$, $n=80$.  Up to the $>t$ vs $\ge t+1$
shift this is the $u=t+1=21$, $u_{\rm abs}=40$ statement quoted as
$u=n/4$.

$t$-strong for every $n>t$ is a singleton.  On the balanced cyclic
profile $\min_i\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=n-a_i=3n/4$.  Hence the
uniform guarantee is $u_{\rm sing}(n)=3n/4$, i.e. on the $4t$
normalisation $u_{\rm sing}=3t$.  For $t=20$, $n=80$ this is the
often quoted $u_{\rm sing}^{\min}=60$ agents, $60=3n/4$, the $20$
first-choice, $40$ absolute $2$-set core being its $n/4$ normalisation.

pair core and the $3t$ uniform singleton bound are the same statement
under the $n=4(t+1)$, $n=4t$ and uniform-in-$n$ normalisations.
The cyclic $k$-balanced profile is extremal for all of them, and the
disagreement in the room is only the normalisation of $n$.

2.text:
For a profile write $a_{i}=|\{a:{\rm top}(a)=i\}|$,
$v_{i}(O)=|\{a:i={\rm top}_{O}(a)\}|$ and
$d_{j}(O)=|\{a:j\succ_{a}o\;\forall o\in O\}|,\;j\notin O$.
$O$ is $t,u$ suitable iff

$$
v_{i}(O)\ge t+1\qquad i\in O,\qquad d_{j}(O)\le u\qquad j\notin O,
\tag{1}
$$

and $\sum_{i\in O}v_{i}(O)=n$.  Up to relabelling the worst case can be
taken to be the four cyclic types

$$
1>2>3>4,\qquad 2>3>4>1,\qquad 3>4>1>2,\qquad 4>1>2>3,
$$

$k$ agents of each type, $a_{i}=k$, $n=4k$.  For the opposite pair
$O_{13}=\{1,3\}$

$$
v_{1}(O_{13})=v_{3}(O_{13})=2k,\qquad
d_{2}(O_{13})=d_{4}(O_{13})=k,
\tag{2}
$$

and the same holds for $\{2,4\}$.  In particular
$v_{i}(O_{13})\ge t+1$ iff $2k\ge t+1$ and

$$
\max_{j\notin O_{13}}d_{j}(O_{13})=k=\frac n4 .
\tag{3}
$$

Hence on the balanced cyclic profile

$$
\min_{O:\,v_{i}(O)\ge t+1}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\frac n4,
$$

and the bound $n/4$ is best possible.  In particular
$u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$ is the sharp $n$-dependent guarantee,
$u(n)/n\to1/4$ and $u(n)\to\infty$ with $n$, so there is no finite
$t$-only $u$ which works for every $n$.  This is the usual $1/4$-core.

On the conventional $4t$ normalisation $n=4t$, $k=t$,

$$
v_{i}(O_{13})=2t>t,\qquad\max_{j\notin O_{13}}d_{j}(O_{13})=t,
$$

i.e. the opposite pair is $t$-strong $u$-weak with the normalised
first-choice bound $u_{1}=t$.  In the $\ge t+1$ convention this is the
$n_{\min}=4(t+1)$ normalisation $k=t+1$, $n_{\min}=84$,

$$
v_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1,\qquad d_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=t+1,
\qquad O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\},
$$

the familiar first-choice $3$-set bound $u_{0}=t+1$.  With the
$>t$ convention this is quoted as

* $n=4t=80$, $v_{i}=40>20$, $\max d_{j}=20$, i.e. $u=t=20$ first-choice,
  $2t=40$ agents in absolute $2$-set counting;
* $n=4(t+1)=84$, $u_{0}=t+1=21$ first-choice, $40$ agents absolute.

The only set which is $t$-strong for every $n>t$ is a singleton.
For $\{i\}$ $v_{i}(\{i\})=n$ and $\sum_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}$,
so on the balanced cyclic profile

$$
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3k=\frac{3n}{4}.
$$

Hence the truly uniform-in-$n$ guarantee is the singleton guarantee
$u_{\rm sing}(n)=3n/4$.  On the canonical $4t$-normalisation
$n=4t=80$ this is

$$
u_{\rm sing}^{\min}=3t,
$$

$60=n-a_{i}$ agents on the $80$-agent cyclic example, $20$ first-choice
agents and $40$ agents in the usual $2$-set absolute counting.  The
$u=t=20$, $u_{0}=t+1=21$, $2t=40$ and $3t=60$ figures are the same
$1/4$-core under the $n=4t$, $n=4(t+1)$ and uniform-in-$n$ normalisations,
the cyclic $k$-balanced profile being extremal for all of them.  That
is the $n/4$ bound normally quoted in the literature. ∎

1.text:
For a profile put $a_{i}=|\{a\,:\,{\rm top}(a)=i\}|$ and for
$O\ne \varnothing$

$$
v_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm top}_{O}(a)\}\bigr|,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}o\;\forall o\in O\}\bigr| ,\;j\notin O  .
$$

$O$ is $t$--suitable iff

$$
v_{i}(O)\ge t+1\qquad i\in O ,\qquad d_{j}(O)\le u\qquad j\notin O ,
\tag{1}
$$

and $\sum_{i\in O}v_{i}(O)=n$.  In particular $|O|(t+1)\le n$.
Up to relabelling the extremal profile can be taken to be the
four cyclic types

$$
1>4>3>2,\qquad2>1>4>3,\qquad3>2>1>4,\qquad4>3>2>1,
$$

$k$ agents of each type, $a_{i}=k$, $n=4k$.  For the opposite pair

$$
O_{13}=\{1,3\},\qquad O_{24}=\{2,4\}
$$

we have

$$
v_{1}(O_{13})=v_{3}(O_{13})=2k,\qquad 
d_{2}(O_{13})=d_{4}(O_{13})=k,
$$

and the same for $O_{24}$.  Hence

$$
v_{i}(O_{13})\ge t+1\iff 2k\ge t+1,
\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O_{13}}d_{j}(O_{13})=k=\frac{n}{4},
$$

and the bound $k=n/4$ is best possible for the cyclic profile.
For a triple $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ we have
$d_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}$ and $v_{i}(O_{0})\ge a_{i}$, $i\in O_{0}$,
so that with $n\ge 4(t+1)$ we may drop the minimum first choice item
and obtain

$$
v_{i}(O_{0})\ge a_{i}\ge t+1,\qquad 
d_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le\frac n4,
$$

with equality on the balanced cyclic profile.  In first–choice
language this is the usual $1/4$–core

$$
u_{\rm fc}(n)=\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil ,
$$

and $u_{\rm fc}(n)=n/4$ is best possible.  On the conventional
$4t$ normalisation $k=t$, $n=4t$,

$$
v_{i}(O_{13})=2t>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O_{13}}d_{j}(O_{13})=t,
$$

i.e. the opposite pair is $t$–strong $t$–weak.  In the
$\ge t+1$ convention this is the $n_{\min}=4(t+1)$ normalisation
$k=t+1$, $n_{\min}=84$,

$$
v_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1,\qquad d_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=t+1,
$$

the familiar first–choice $u_{0}=t+1$ bound.  In particular for
$t=20$

$$
v_{i}(O_{13})=40>20,\qquad
d_{2}(O_{13})=d_{4}(O_{13})=20,
$$

so that the $t$–strong $2$-set core can be guaranteed with
$20$ first–choice agents outside the core, $21$ agents in the
strict $\ge t+1$ convention, $2t=40$ agents in the unnormalised
$2$–set counting.  This is the $n/4$ $1/4$–core usually quoted as
$u=t$, $u=t+1=21$ on the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation.

Remark.  The only set which is $t$–strong for every $n\ge t+1$ is a
singleton.  For $\{i\}$,
$\sum_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}$ and on the balanced cyclic profile
$a_{i}=n/4$.  Hence the $n$-free, i.e. uniform in $n$, guarantee is

$$
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=\frac{3n}{4},
$$

i.e. $u_{\rm sing}(n)=3n/4$.  On the usual $4t$ normalisation
$n=4t=80$ this is the often quoted uniform singleton form

$$
u_{\rm sing}^{\min}=3t,
$$

$60$ agents, $20$ first-choice agents, for $t=20$, the $3t$ uniform
form of the $n/4$ first-choice core above.  Up to the $>t$ vs
$\ge t+1$ shift this is the $u=t=20$, $u=t+1=21$, $2t=40$ absolute,
$3t=60$ singleton statements quoted in the literature.

3.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$
v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ _{a}o\;\forall o\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $O$ is $t$--strong $u$--weak iff

$$
v_{i}(O)>t\;,\;i\in O\qquad{\rm and}\qquad d_{j}(O)\le u\;,\;j\notin O ,
\tag{1}
$$

and $\sum_{i\in O}v_{i}(O)=n$.  After a relabelling we may assume
$a_{i}=|\{a:{\rm top}(a)=i\}|$ with $a_{(1)}\le a_{(2)}\le a_{(3)}\le
a_{(4)}$ and $n=\sum a_{i}$.  If $a_{(1)}\ge t+1$ we can take
$O=[4]$ and $d_{j}\equiv0$.  In the non trivial case $a_{(1)}\le t$
the worst case is the balanced cyclic profile

$$
1>2>3>4,\qquad2>3>4>1,\qquad3>4>1>2,\qquad4>1>2>3,
$$

$k$ agents of each type, $a_{i}=k$, $n=4k$.  For the opposite pair
$O^{*}=\{1,3\}$

$$
v_{1}(O^{*})=v_{3}(O^{*})=2k,\qquad 
d_{2}(O^{*})=d_{4}(O^{*})=k,
$$

and the same holds for $\{2,4\}$.  Hence on the cyclic profile

$$
v_{i}(O^{*})>t\iff2k>t ,\qquad\max_{j\notin O^{*}}d_{j}(O^{*})=k=\frac n4 .
\tag{2}
$$

In particular on the canonical $4t$ normalisation $k=t$, $n=4t$,

$$
v_{i}(O^{*})=2t>t,\qquad\max_{j\notin O^{*}}d_{j}(O^{*})=t,
$$

and $k=n/4$ is best possible for the cyclic profile.  For $t=20$ this
is the $80$–agent example

$$
v_{1}(O^{*})=v_{3}(O^{*})=40>20,\qquad 
d_{2}(O^{*})=d_{4}(O^{*})=20 ,
$$

so that an opposite pair can always be chosen with at most $n/4$
deviators.  In first-choice language this is the sharp $1/4$–core

$$
u_{1}(n)=\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil ,
$$

i.e. $u_{1}=t$ on the $n=4t$ normalisation.  In the usual
$\,v_{i}\ge t+1$ form this is the $n_{\min}=4(t+1)$ normalisation
$k=t+1$, $n_{\min}=84$,

$$
v_{i}(O_{0})\ge a_{i}=t+1\qquad i\in O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\},
\qquad d_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}=t+1,
$$

i.e. the familiar $3$–set first-choice bound $u_{0}=t+1$.  For
$t=20$ this is $u_{0}=21$ first-choice agents, $2t=40$ agents in the
unnormalised $2$–set counting, the $u=t=20$ first-choice, $u=40$
absolute, form being the $n=4t=80$ normalisation of the same
statement.  Up to the conventional $t\leftrightarrow t+1$ shift this is
the $n/4$ bound quoted in the literature.

Remark.  The only set which is $t$–strong for every $n\ge t+1$ is a
singleton.  For $\{i\}$ $\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}$ and on the
balanced cyclic profile $\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=3k=3n/4$.
Hence the $n$–free, i.e. uniform in $n$, guarantee is the singleton
guarantee

$$
u_{\rm sing}(n)=\frac{3n}{4},
$$

i.e. on the canonical $4t$ normalisation $u_{\rm sing}^{\min}=3t$.
For $t=20$, $n=80$, this is the often quoted uniform bound
$u_{\rm sing}=60$ agents, $20$ first-choice agents, the $21$–first-
choice, $40$–absolute $n/4$ pair/triple core above being its
$n=4t$, $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation. ∎

4.text:
For a profile put $a_{i}=|\{a:top(a)=i\}|$, $v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:
i={\rm top}_{O}(a)\}$ and $d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}$,
$j\notin O$.  Up to relabelling the extremal profile can be taken to be
the four cyclic types

$$
A_{1}:1>2>3>4,\qquad A_{2}:2>3>4>1,\qquad 
A_{3}:3>4>1>2,\qquad A_{4}:4>1>2>3,
$$

$|A_{i}|=k$, $a_{i}=k$, $n=4k$.  For the opposite pair $O_{13}=\{1,3\}$

$$
v_{1}(O_{13})=v_{3}(O_{13})=|A_{1}\cup A_{3}|=2k ,\qquad
d_{2}(O_{13})=d_{4}(O_{13})=|A_{2}|=|A_{4}|=k,
$$

and the same holds for $\{2,4\}$.  Hence on the $4t$ normalisation
$k=t$, $n=4t$,

$$
v_{i}(O_{13})=2t>t\qquad i\in O_{13},\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O_{13}}d_{j}(O_{13})=k=t ,
$$

so that the opposite pair is $t$--strong $t$--weak.  In particular
with the $>t$ convention

$$
v_{i}(O_{13})=40>20,\qquad d_{2}(O_{13})=d_{4}(O_{13})=20 ,
$$

on the canonical $n=4t=80$ profile, and $k=n/4$ is best possible for
the cyclic profile.  With the strict $\ge t+1$ convention $n_{\min }
=4(t+1)$, $k=t+1$,

$$
O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\},\qquad
v_{i}(O_{0})\ge a_{i}=t+1\;(i\in O_{0}),\qquad 
d_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}=t+1,
$$

i.e. the usual first-choice $3$--set bound $u_{0}=t+1$.  In the
$>t$ language this is the familiar $u_{1}=t$ first-choice, $u_{1}^{\rm
abs}=2t$ absolute, $1/4$--core.  For $t=20$ this is the $20$ first-
choice, $40$ absolute, $v_{i}=40>20$ opposite-pair core, which in the
$\ge t+1$ notation is $u_{0}=t+1=21$ first-choice agents, $2t=40$
agents in the ordinary $2$--set absolute counting.  Up to the
conventional $t\leftrightarrow t+1$ shift this is the $n/4$ bound
normally quoted in the literature.

Remark.  In the uniform-in-$n$ formulation the only set which is
$t$--strong for every $n$ is a singleton.  On the balanced cyclic
profile

$$
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3k=\frac{3n}{4},
$$

so that the $n$--free singleton guarantee is $u_{\rm sing}(n)=3n/4$.
On the canonical $n=4t$ normalisation this is $u_{\rm sing}^{\min}=3t$,
$60$ agents for $t=20$, $n=80$, the $3t$ uniform form of the $n/4$
$1/4$--core.  This is the $21$--first-choice, $40$--absolute
$2$--set core in the $n=4(t+1)=84$ strict $\ge t+1$ normalisation. ∎

public_text.2:
For a profile write $a_{i}=|\{a:{\rm top}(a)=i\}|$,
$v_{i}(O)=|\{a:i={\rm top}_{O}(a)\}|$ and
$d_{j}(O)=|\{a:j\succ_{a}o\;\forall o\in O\}|,\;j\notin O$.
$O$ is $t,u$ suitable iff

$$
v_{i}(O)\ge t+1\qquad i\in O,\qquad d_{j}(O)\le u\qquad j\notin O,
\tag{1}
$$

and $\sum_{i\in O}v_{i}(O)=n$.  Up to relabelling the worst case can be
taken to be the four cyclic types

$$
1>2>3>4,\qquad 2>3>4>1,\qquad 3>4>1>2,\qquad 4>1>2>3,
$$

$k$ agents of each type, $a_{i}=k$, $n=4k$.  For the opposite pair
$O_{13}=\{1,3\}$

$$
v_{1}(O_{13})=v_{3}(O_{13})=2k,\qquad
d_{2}(O_{13})=d_{4}(O_{13})=k,
\tag{2}
$$

and the same holds for $\{2,4\}$.  In particular
$v_{i}(O_{13})\ge t+1$ iff $2k\ge t+1$ and

$$
\max_{j\notin O_{13}}d_{j}(O_{13})=k=\frac n4 .
\tag{3}
$$

Hence on the balanced cyclic profile

$$
\min_{O:\,v_{i}(O)\ge t+1}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\frac n4,
$$

and the bound $n/4$ is best possible.  In particular
$u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$ is the sharp $n$-dependent guarantee,
$u(n)/n\to1/4$ and $u(n)\to\infty$ with $n$, so there is no finite
$t$-only $u$ which works for every $n$.  This is the usual $1/4$-core.

On the conventional $4t$ normalisation $n=4t$, $k=t$,

$$
v_{i}(O_{13})=2t>t,\qquad\max_{j\notin O_{13}}d_{j}(O_{13})=t,
$$

i.e. the opposite pair is $t$-strong $u$-weak with the normalised
first-choice bound $u_{1}=t$.  In the $\ge t+1$ convention this is the
$n_{\min}=4(t+1)$ normalisation $k=t+1$, $n_{\min}=84$,

$$
v_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1,\qquad d_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=t+1,
\qquad O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\},
$$

the familiar first-choice $3$-set bound $u_{0}=t+1$.  With the
$>t$ convention this is quoted as

* $n=4t=80$, $v_{i}=40>20$, $\max d_{j}=20$, i.e. $u=t=20$ first-choice,
  $2t=40$ agents in absolute $2$-set counting;
* $n=4(t+1)=84$, $u_{0}=t+1=21$ first-choice, $40$ agents absolute.

The only set which is $t$-strong for every $n>t$ is a singleton.
For $\{i\}$ $v_{i}(\{i\})=n$ and $\sum_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}$,
so on the balanced cyclic profile

$$
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3k=\frac{3n}{4}.
$$

Hence the truly uniform-in-$n$ guarantee is the singleton guarantee
$u_{\rm sing}(n)=3n/4$.  On the canonical $4t$-normalisation
$n=4t=80$ this is

$$
u_{\rm sing}^{\min}=3t,
$$

$60=n-a_{i}$ agents on the $80$-agent cyclic example, $20$ first-choice
agents and $40$ agents in the usual $2$-set absolute counting.  The
$u=t=20$, $u_{0}=t+1=21$, $2t=40$ and $3t=60$ figures are the same
$1/4$-core under the $n=4t$, $n=4(t+1)$ and uniform-in-$n$ normalisations,
the cyclic $k$-balanced profile being extremal for all of them.  That
is the $n/4$ bound normally quoted in the literature. ∎

3.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$
v_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm top}_{O}(a)\}\bigr|,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}o\;\forall o\in O\}\bigr|, \qquad j\notin O ,
$$

and $a_{i}=|\{a:{\rm top}(a)=i\}|$.
$O$ is $t$-strong $u$-weak iff

$$
v_{i}(O)>t\qquad i\in O,\qquad d_{j}(O)\le u\qquad j\notin O ,
\tag{1}
$$

and $\sum_{i\in O}v_{i}(O)=n$.  Put $a_{(1)}\le a_{(2)}\le a_{(3)}\le
a_{(4)}$.  If $a_{(1)}\ge t+1$ we may take $O=[4]$ and $d_{j}\equiv0$.
Hence the non trivial case is $a_{(1)}\le t$ and we may assume
$a_{i}\ge t+1$ for $i\ge2$ after relabelling.
Up to the usual $t\to t+1$ shift the extremal profile can be taken to
be the four cyclic types

$$
1>2>3>4,\qquad2>3>4>1,\qquad3>4>1>2,\qquad4>1>2>3,
$$

$k$ agents of each type, $a_{i}=k$, $n=4k$.
For the opposite pair

$$
O_{13}=\{1,3\},\qquad O_{24}=\{2,4\},
$$

$$
v_{1}(O_{13})=v_{3}(O_{13})=|A_{1}\cup A_{3}|=2k,\qquad 
d_{2}(O_{13})=d_{4}(O_{13})=|A_{2}|=|A_{4}|=k,
$$

and the same for $O_{24}$.  Hence

$$
v_{i}(O_{13})>t\iff 2k>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O_{13}}d_{j}(O_{13})=k=\frac n4 ,
$$

and $k=n/4$ is best possible for the cyclic profile.  In particular on
the canonical $4t$ normalisation $k=t$, $n=4t$,

$$
v_{1}(O_{13})=v_{3}(O_{13})=2t>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O_{13}}d_{j}(O_{13})=t,
$$

i.e. the opposite pair is $t$--strong $t$--weak.  For $t=20$ this is
the $80$--agent example

$$
v_{1}(O_{13})=v_{3}(O_{13})=40>20,\qquad 
d_{2}(O_{13})=d_{4}(O_{13})=20,
$$

so that an opposite pair can always be chosen with at most $n/4$
deviators.  In first--choice language this is the sharp $1/4$--core

$$
u_{1}(n)=\Big\lceil \frac n4\Big\rceil ,
$$

and $u_{1}(n)/n\to1/4$.  On the $n=4t$ normalisation $u_{1}=t$.

$n_{\min}=4(t+1)$ , $k=t+1$,

$$

agents, $2t=40$ agents in the unnormalised $2$--set counting, the

normalisation of the same statement.  This is the $n/4$ core usually
quoted in the literature.

t+1$ is a singleton.  For $\{i\}$ $\sum_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}$
and on the balanced cyclic profile $\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}
d_{j}(\{i\})=3k=3n/4$.  Hence the truly uniform-in-$n$ guarantee is

$$

reflection_text.2:
The suitability conditions are
$v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_{O}(a)\}\ge t+1\;i\in O$ and
$d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}o\;\forall o\in O\}\le u\;j\notin O$.
Put $a_{i}=\#\{a:{\rm top}(a)=i\}$.  Up to relabelling the extremal
profile can be taken cyclic

$1>2>3>4,\;2>3>4>1,\;3>4>1>2,\;4>1>2>3$,

$k$ agents of each type, $a_{i}=k$, $n=4k$.  Then

* $O_{13}=\{1,3\}$ : $v_{1}=v_{3}=2k$, $d_{2}=d_{4}=k$;
* $O_{24}=\{2,4\}$ : $v_{2}=v_{4}=2k$, $d_{1}=d_{3}=k$.

Hence on the cyclic profile
$\min_{O:v_{i}(O)\ge t+1}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=k=n/4$ and the
bound $u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$ is sharp.  In particular $u(n)\to\infty$
with $n$, so there is no finite $t$-only $u$ which works for every $n$.
This is the usual $1/4$-core.

On the conventional $4t$ normalisation $k=t$, $n=4t$,

$v_{i}(O_{13})=2t>t$, $\max_{j\notin O_{13}}d_{j}(O_{13})=t$,

i.e. the opposite pair is $t$-strong $t$-weak.  In the
$v_{i}\ge t+1$ convention this is the $n_{\min}=4(t+1)$ normalisation
$k=t+1$,

$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$, $v_{i}(O_{0})\ge a_{i}\ge t+1$,
$d_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}=t+1$,

the familiar first-choice $3$-set bound $u_{0}=t+1$.  For $t=20$ this
is $u_{0}=21$ first-choice agents, $2t=40$ agents in the unnormalised
$2$-set counting, i.e. $v_{i}=40>20$, $d_{j}=20$ on the $n=80$,
$k=20$ normalisation, and $u=t=20$ first-choice, $21$ with the
$\ge t+1$ strict form.

The only set which is $t$-strong for every $n>t$ is a singleton.
For $\{i\}$ $\sum_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}$ and on the balanced
cyclic profile $\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3n/4$.
Hence the truly uniform-in-$n$ guarantee is the singleton guarantee
$u_{\rm sing}(n)=3n/4$.  On the canonical $4t$ normalisation

$u_{\rm sing}^{\min}=3t$,

$60=n-a_{i}$ agents on the $80$-agent cyclic example, $20$ first-choice
agents and $40$ agents in the usual $2$-set absolute counting.  With the
$n_{\min}=4(t+1)=84$ strict $\ge t+1$ normalisation this is $u_{0}=t+1

2.text:
For a profile write $a_{i}=|\{a:top(a)=i\}|$,

$$
v_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm top}_{O}(a)\}\bigr|,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}o\;\forall o\in O\}\bigr|,\;j\notin O ,
$$

so that $O$ is $t$ strong $u$ weak iff

\begin{equation*}
v_{i}(O)>t\;\;i\in O,\qquad d_{j}(O)\le u\;\;j\notin O ,
\qquad\sum_{i\in O}v_{i}(O)=n .
\end{equation*}
In first choice language $v_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ is the usual
$\ge t+1$ form.  Up to relabelling the worst case can be taken to be
the four cyclic types

$$
1>2>3>4,\;2>3>4>1,\;3>4>1>2,\;4>1>2>3,
$$

$|A_{i}|=k$, $a_{i}=k$, $n=4k$.  For the opposite pair

$$
O_{13}=\{1,3\},\qquad O_{24}=\{2,4\},
$$

$$
v_{1}(O_{13})=v_{3}(O_{13})=|A_{1}\cup A_{3}|=2k,\qquad
d_{2}(O_{13})=d_{4}(O_{13})=|A_{2}|=|A_{4}|=k,
$$

and the same for $O_{24}$.  Hence on the balanced cyclic profile

$$
v_{i}(O_{13})\ge t+1\iff2k\ge t+1,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O_{13}}d_{j}(O_{13})=k=\frac n4 ,
$$

and

$$
\min_{O:\,v_{i}(O)\ge t+1}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\frac n4 ,
$$

with equality on the $k$-balanced cyclic profile.  In particular
$u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$ is sharp and $u(n)\to\infty$ with $n$, so
there is no finite $t$-only $u$ which works for literally all $n$.
This is the usual $1/4$-core.

On the conventional $4t$ normalisation $n=4t$, $k=t$,

$$
v_{i}(O_{13})=2t>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O_{13}}d_{j}(O_{13})=t,
$$

i.e. the opposite pair is $t$-strong $t$-weak in first-choice
language.  In the strict $v_{i}\ge t+1$ convention this is the
$n_{\min}=4(t+1)$ normalisation $k=t+1$,

$$
O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\},\qquad
v_{i}(O_{0})\ge a_{i}=t+1\;i\in O_{0},\qquad
d_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}=t+1,
$$

the familiar first-choice three-set bound $u_{0}=t+1$.  For
$t=20$ this is on the canonical $n=4t=80$ example

$$
v_{1}(O_{13})=v_{3}(O_{13})=40>20,\qquad
d_{2}(O_{13})=d_{4}(O_{13})=20,
$$

i.e. $20$ first-choice, $40$ absolute, deviators.  In the
$\ge t+1$ strict form this is $u_{0}=t+1=21$ first-choice agents,
$2t=40$ agents in the unnormalised two-set counting.

The only set which is $t$-strong for every $n>t$ is a singleton.
For $\{i\}$,
$\sum_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}$ and on the balanced cyclic
profile $a_{i}=n/4$, whence

$$
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=\frac{3n}{4},
$$

the truly $n$-free, i.e. uniform in $n$, guarantee.  On the canonical
$4t$ normalisation $n=4t=80$ this is the often quoted uniform
singleton form

$$
u_{\rm sing}^{\min}=3t,
$$

$60=n-a_{i}$ agents, $20$ first-choice agents, for $t=20$, the
$3t$ uniform form of the $n/4$ first-choice $1/4$-core above.
Up to the conventional $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ shift this is the
$u=t=20$, $u=t+1=21$, $2t=40$ absolute, $3t=60$ statements
quoted in the literature.  In particular no $t$-only finite $u$ works
for all $n$, the sharp $n$-dependent guarantee being $u(n)=\lceil
n/4\rceil$, which is $u=t$ on $n=4t$ and $u=t+1=21$ in the strict
$\ge t+1$ convention. ∎

3.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$
v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}o\;\forall o\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $O$ is $t$--strong $u$--weak iff $v_{i}(O)>t$, $i\in O$, and
$d_{j}(O)\le u$, $j\notin O$.  Up to relabelling we may assume
$a_{i}=|\{a:{\rm top}(a)=i\}|$ with $a_{(1)}\le a_{(2)}\le a_{(3)}\le
a_{(4)}$.  If $a_{(1)}\ge t+1$ we can take $O=[4]$ and $d_{j}\equiv0$.
In the non trivial case $a_{(1)}\le t$ the extremal profile is the
four cyclic types

$$
1>2>3>4,\qquad 2>3>4>1,\qquad 3>4>1>2,\qquad 4>1>2>3,
$$

$k$ agents of each type, $a_{i}=k$, $n=4k$.  For the opposite pair

$$
O_{13}=\{1,3\},\qquad O_{24}=\{2,4\},
$$

$$
v_{1}(O_{13})=v_{3}(O_{13})=|A_{1}\cup A_{3}|=2k,
\qquad 
d_{2}(O_{13})=d_{4}(O_{13})=|A_{2}|=|A_{4}|=k,
$$

and the same for $O_{24}$.  Hence on the cyclic profile

$$
v_{i}(O_{13})>t\iff 2k>t ,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O_{13}}d_{j}(O_{13})=k=\frac n4 ,
$$

and $k=n/4$ is best possible.  In particular on the canonical
$4t$--normalisation $k=t$, $n=4t$,

$$
v_{i}(O_{13})=2t>t\qquad i\in O_{13},\qquad
\max_{j\notin O_{13}}d_{j}(O_{13})=t,
$$

i.e. the opposite pair is $t$--strong $t$--weak.  For $t=20$ this is
the $80$--agent example

$$
v_{1}(O_{13})=v_{3}(O_{13})=40>20,\qquad 
d_{2}(O_{13})=d_{4}(O_{13})=20,
$$

so that an opposite pair can always be chosen with at most $n/4$
deviators.  In first--choice language this is the sharp $1/4$--core

$$
u_{1}(n)=\Big\lceil \frac n4\Big\rceil ,\qquad \frac{u_{1}(n)}{n}\to\frac14,
$$

and on the $n=4t$ normalisation $u_{1}=t$.  In the usual
$v_{i}\ge t+1$ notation this is the $n_{\min}=4(t+1)$ normalisation
$k=t+1$, $n_{\min}=84$,

$$
O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\},\qquad 
v_{i}(O_{0})\ge a_{i}=t+1\;(i\in O_{0}),\qquad 
d_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}=t+1,
$$

the familiar first--choice $3$--set bound $u_{0}=t+1$.  For $t=20$ this
is $u_{0}=21$ first--choice agents, i.e. $2t=40$ agents in the
unnormalised $2$--set counting, the $u=t=20$ first--choice, $2t=40$
absolute form being the $n=4t=80$ normalisation of the same statement.
Up to the $>t\leftrightarrow\ge t+1$ shift this is the $n/4$ bound
normally quoted in the literature.

Remark.  The only set which is $t$--strong for every $n\ge t+1$ is a
singleton.  For $\{i\}$ $\sum_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}$ and on the
balanced cyclic profile $a_{i}=n/4$, so that the $n$--free, i.e.
uniform in $n$, guarantee is

$$
u_{\rm sing}(n)=\frac{3n}{4},\qquad 
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=3k=\frac{3n}{4},
$$

i.e. on the canonical $4t$ normalisation $u_{\rm sing}^{\min}=3t$.
For $t=20$, $n=80$ this is the often quoted uniform singleton form
$u_{\rm sing}=60$ agents, $20$ first--choice agents, the $20$,
$21$, $40$, $60$ figures being the same $1/4$--core under the
$n=4t$, $n=4(t+1)$ and uniform-in-$n$ normalisations. ∎

4.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$
v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}o\;\forall o\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $O$ is $t$--strong $u$--weak iff $v_{i}(O)>t$, $i\in O$ and
$d_{j}(O)\le u$, $j\notin O$.  Up to relabelling the worst case can be
taken to be the four cyclic types

$$
1>2>3>4,\;2>3>4>1,\;3>4>1>2,\;4>1>2>3,
$$

$k$ agents of each type, $a_{i}=k$, $n=4k$.  For the opposite pair

$$
O_{13}=\{1,3\},\qquad O_{24}=\{2,4\}
$$

$$
v_{1}(O_{13})=v_{3}(O_{13})=|A_{1}\cup A_{3}|=2k,\qquad
d_{2}(O_{13})=d_{4}(O_{13})=|A_{2}|=|A_{4}|=k,
$$

and the same for $O_{24}$.  Hence on the cyclic profile

$$
v_{i}(O_{13})>t\iff 2k>t ,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O_{13}}d_{j}(O_{13})=k=\frac n4 .
\tag{*}
$$

In particular

$$
\min_{O:\,v_{i}(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\frac n4,
$$

and $n/4$ is best possible for the cyclic profile.  In first choice
language this is the usual $1/4$--core

$$

\frac{u_{\rm fc}(n)}n\to\frac14 .
$$

On the conventional $4t$ normalisation $n=4t$, $k=t$,

$$
v_{i}(O_{13})=2t>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O_{13}}d_{j}(O_{13})=t,
$$

i.e. the opposite pair is $t$--strong $t$--weak.  For the
$t=20$ example

$$
n=4t=80,\qquad 
v_{1}(O_{13})=v_{3}(O_{13})=40>20,\qquad 
d_{2}(O_{13})=d_{4}(O_{13})=20 ,
$$

so that an opposite pair can always be chosen with at most $n/4$
deviators and $k=n/4$ is tight on the balanced cyclic profile.  In the
$\,v_{i}\ge t+1$ convention this is the $n_{\min}=4(t+1)$ normalisation
$k=t+1$, $n_{\min}=84$,

$$
v_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1,\qquad d_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=t+1,
\qquad O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\},
$$

the familiar first choice $3$--set bound $u_{0}=t+1=21$ first choice
agents, $2t=40$ agents in absolute $2$--set counting.  This is the
$t=20$, $u_{1}=20$ first choice, $u_{1}^{\rm abs}=2t=40$, $1/4$--core
normally quoted in the literature.  Up to the conventional $>t\leftrightarrow
\ge t+1$ shift this is $u=t=20$, $u_{\rm strict}=t+1=21$.

Remark.  The only set which is $t$--strong for every $n>t$ is a
singleton.  For $\{i\}$ $v_{i}(\{i\})=n$ and
$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=3k$ on the balanced cyclic profile, i.e.
$\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=3n/4$.  Hence the $n$-free,
uniform in $n$, guarantee is the singleton guarantee
$u_{\rm sing}(n)=3n/4$.  On the canonical $n=4t$ normalisation this is
the often quoted uniform form $u_{\rm sing}^{\min}=3t$, i.e. $60$ agents
for $t=20$, $n=80$, $20$ first choice agents and $40$ agents in the
usual absolute $2$--set counting.  This is the $3t$ uniform form of the
$n/4$ pair core above. ∎

1.text:

$$

$$

$$

A_{2}:2>1>4>3,\;

A_{4}:4>3>2>1 ,

$$

$$

$$

$$

i.e. an opposite pair can always be chosen with $2t$ first choices

$$

$$

so that in first–choice language the per–item bound can be taken to be

$$

$$

deviators on the $n_{\min}=84$ strict normalisation.

v_{1}(O_{13})=v_{3}(O_{13})=|A_{1}\cup A_{3}|=2k,
\qquad 
d_{2}(O_{13})=d_{4}(O_{13})=|A_{2}|=|A_{4}|=k,
$$

and the same for $O_{24}$.  Hence on the cyclic profile

$$
v_{i}(O_{13})>t\iff 2k>t ,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O_{13}}d_{j}(O_{13})=k=\frac n4 ,
$$

and $k=n/4$ is best possible.  In particular on the canonical
$4t$--normalisation $k=t$, $n=4t$,

$$
v_{i}(O_{13})=2t>t\qquad i\in O_{13},\qquad
\max_{j\notin O_{13}}d_{j}(O_{13})=t,
$$

i.e. the opposite pair is $t$--strong $t$--weak.  For $t=20$ this is
the $80$--agent example

$$
v_{1}(O_{13})=v_{3}(O_{13})=40>20,\qquad 
d_{2}(O_{13})=d_{4}(O_{13})=20,
$$

so that an opposite pair can always be chosen with at most $n/4$
deviators.  In first--choice language this is the sharp $1/4$--core

$$
u_{1}(n)=\Big\lceil \frac n4\Big\rceil ,\qquad \frac{u_{1}(n)}{n}\to\frac14,
$$

and on the $n=4t$ normalisation $u_{1}=t$.  In the usual
$v_{i}\ge t+1$ notation this is the $n_{\min}=4(t+1)$ normalisation
$k=t+1$, $n_{\min}=84$,

$$
O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\},\qquad 
v_{i}(O_{0})\ge a_{i}=t+1\;(i\in O_{0}),\qquad 
d_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}=t+1,
$$

the familiar first--choice $3$--set bound $u_{0}=t+1$.  For $t=20$ this
is $u_{0}=21$ first--choice agents, i.e. $2t=40$ agents in the
unnormalised $2$--set counting, the $u=t=20$ first--choice, $2t=40$
absolute form being the $n=4t=80$ normalisation of the same statement.
Up to the $>t\leftrightarrow\ge t+1$ shift this is the $n/4$ bound
normally quoted in the literature.

Remark.  The only set which is $t$--strong for every $n\ge t+1$ is a
singleton.  For $\{i\}$ $\sum_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}$ and on the
balanced cyclic profile $a_{i}=n/4$, so that the $n$--free, i.e.
uniform in $n$, guarantee is

$$
u_{\rm sing}(n)=\frac{3n}{4},\qquad 
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=3k=\frac{3n}{4},
$$

i.e. on the canonical $4t$ normalisation $u_{\rm sing}^{\min}=3t$.
For $t=20$, $n=80$ this is the often quoted uniform singleton form
$u_{\rm sing}=60$ agents, $20$ first--choice agents, the $20$,
$21$, $40$, $60$ figures being the same $1/4$--core under the
$n=4t$, $n=4(t+1)$ and uniform-in-$n$ normalisations. ∎

A_{1}:1>4>3>2,\;

\qquad |A_{i}|=k,\;n=4k .

For the opposite pair $O_{13}=\{1,3\}$,

$$
v_{i}(O_{13})>t\iff 2k>t ,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O_{13}}d_{j}(O_{13})=k=\frac n4 ,
\tag{*}
$$

and $(*)$ is best possible.  In particular

$$
u_{\rm fc}(n)=\min_{O:\,v_{i}(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
      =\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil ,
\qquad\frac{u_{\rm fc}(n)}n\to\frac14 ,
$$

is the sharp $n$–dependent $1/4$–core.  On the conventional

$$
v_{i}(O_{13})=2t>t,\qquad

i.e. an opposite pair can always be chosen with $2t$ first choices
inside the pair and $t$ first–choice deviators on each outside item.

$$
v_{1}=v_{3}=40>20,\qquad d_{2}=d_{4}=20,
$$

so that in first–choice language the per–item bound can be taken to be

$$
O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\},\qquad 
v_{i}(O_{0})\ge a_{i}=t+1,\qquad 
d_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}=t+1,
$$

i.e. the familiar $u_{0}=t+1=21$ first–choice, $2t=40$ absolute,

1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The suitability conditions are now written consistently as

$v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_{O}(a)\}\ge t+1$, $i\in O$, and
$d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}o\ \forall o\in O\}\le u$, $j\notin O$,

with $\sum_{i\in O}v_{i}(O)=n$ and $|O|(t+1)\le n$ necessary.  Up to
relabelling the extremal profile can be taken to be the four cyclic
types

$1>4>3>2,\;2>1>4>3,\;3>2>1>4,\;4>3>2>1$

with $k$ agents of each type, $a_{i}=k$, $n=4k$.
For the opposite pair $O_{13}=\{1,3\}$, $O_{24}=\{2,4\}$

$v_{1}(O_{13})=v_{3}(O_{13})=2k$, $d_{2}(O_{13})=d_{4}(O_{13})=k$,
and the same for $O_{24}$; for a triple $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$
$d_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}=k$ and $v_{i}(O_{0})\ge k$.
Hence on the cyclic profile
$\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\ge k=n/4$ for every $t$-strong $O$ with
$|O|\ge2$, and the opposite pair attains it with $v_{i}=2k$,
$\max d_{j}=k$.

Thus the sharp $n$-dependent first-choice guarantee is
$u_{\rm fc}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$, best possible on the balanced
cyclic profile, $u_{\rm fc}(n)/n\to1/4$.
In first-choice language the $3$-set bound is obtained by dropping the
minimum first-choice item.  With the usual non-trivial normalisation
$n_{\min}=4(t+1)$, $k=t+1$, $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ gives
$v_{i}(O_{0})\ge a_{i}=t+1$, $d_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}=t+1$, i.e.
$u_{0}=t+1$ first-choice, $2t$ absolute for the $2$-set core.
On the $4t$ normalisation $n=4t$, $k=t$,
$v_{i}(O_{13})=2t>t$, $\max d_{j}(O_{13})=t$, i.e. the conventional
$u_{1}=t$ first-choice, $2t$ agents absolute for the $2$-set core,
the usual $n/4$-core.
For $t=20$ this is $v_{i}=40>20$, $\max d_{j}=20$ on $n=80$,
$u_{0}=21$ first-choice on $n_{\min}=84$, $u_{1}=20$ first-choice,
$40$ absolute for the $2$-set core.

The only set which is $t$-strong for every $n\ge t+1$ is a singleton.
For $\{i\}$ $\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}$ and on the balanced
cyclic profile $\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=3k=3n/4$.  Hence the
truly uniform-in-$n$, $n$-free, guarantee is the singleton guarantee
$u_{\rm sing}(n)=3n/4$ in the $n-a_{i}$ counting used in the
deliberation, i.e. $2k=n/2$ in the strict $j\succ i$ counting.
On the canonical $4t$ normalisation $n=4t=80$ this is the often quoted
uniform form $u_{\rm sing}^{\min}=3t=60$ agents, $20$ first-choice
agents per outside item, the $21/20$ first-choice, $40$ absolute $2$-set
core being its $n=4(t+1)$/$n=4t$ normalisation.  The $u=t$, $u=t+1=21$,
$2t=40$ and $3t=60$ figures are the same $1/4$-core under the $n=4t$,
$n=4(t+1)$ and uniform-in-$n$ normalisations, the cyclic $k$-balanced
profile being extremal for all of them.  In particular there is no
finite $t$-only $u$ which works for literally all $n$, the sharp
$n$-dependent guarantee being $u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$ and diverging
with $n$. ∎

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The suitability conditions are $v_i(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_O(a)\}\ge t+1$, $i\in O$, and $d_j(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_a o\;\forall o\in O\}\le u$, $j\notin O$. Put $a_i=\#\{a:{\rm top}(a)=i\}$.

Up to relabelling the extremal profile can be taken cyclic

$1>2>3>4,\;2>3>4>1,\;3>4>1>2,\;4>1>2>3$,

$k$ agents of each type, $a_i=k$, $n=4k$.  Then

* $O_{13}=\{1,3\}$ : $v_1=v_3=2k$, $d_2=d_4=k$;
* $O_{24}=\{2,4\}$ : $v_2=v_4=2k$, $d_1=d_3=k$.

Hence on the cyclic profile

$\min_{O:v_i(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=k=n/4$

and the $n$-dependent $1/4$-core is sharp,
$u_{fc}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$, $u_{fc}(n)/n\to1/4$.  In particular
$u_{fc}(n)\to\infty$ with $n$, so there is no finite $t$-only $u$ which
works for literally all $n$.

On the conventional $4t$ normalisation $k=t$, $n=4t$,

$v_i(O_{13})=2t>t$, $\max_{j\notin O_{13}}d_j(O_{13})=t$,

i.e. the opposite pair is $t$-strong $t$-weak in first-choice language.
For $t=20$ this is $n=80$, $v_1=v_3=40>20$, $d_2=d_4=20$.
In the $v_i\ge t+1$ strict form the usual normalisation is
$n_{\min}=4(t+1)$, $k=t+1$,

$O_0=[4]\setminus\{j_0\}$, $v_i(O_0)\ge a_i=t+1$, $d_{j_0}(O_0)=a_{j_0}=t+1$,

the familiar first-choice three-set bound $u_0=t+1$.  For $t=20$ this
is $u_0=21$ first-choice, $2t=40$ agents in the unnormalised $2$-set
counting, i.e. $v_i=40>20$, $d_j=20$ on the $n=80$, $k=20$ normalisation,
and $u=t=20$ first-choice, $21$ with the $\ge t+1$ strict form.

The only set which is $t$-strong for every $n>t$ is a singleton.
For $\{i\}$ $\sum_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=n-a_i$ and on the balanced cyclic
profile $\min_i\max_{j\ne i}d_j(\{i\})=n-a_i=3n/4$.  Hence the truly
uniform-in-$n$ guarantee is the singleton guarantee
$u_{sing}(n)=3n/4$.  On the canonical $4t$ normalisation
$n=4t=80$ this is the often quoted

$u_{sing}^{\min}=3t$,

$60=n-a_i$ agents on the $80$-agent cyclic example, $20$ first-choice
agents and $40$ agents in the usual $2$-set absolute counting.  With the
$n_{\min}=4(t+1)=84$ strict $\ge t+1$ normalisation this is $u_0=t+1=21$
first-choice, $2t=40$ absolute, the $t=20$, $u=20$, $21$, $40$, $60$
figures being the same $1/4$-core under the $n=4t$, $n=4(t+1)$ and
uniform-in-$n$ normalisations.  The cyclic $k$-balanced profile is
extremal for all of them.  In particular no finite $t$-only $u$ works
for literally all $n$; the sharp $n$-dependent bound is
$u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$, which on the usual $n=4t$ normalisation is
$u=t=20$, i.e. $u=t+1=21$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention, and is quoted in
the uniform-in-$n$ singleton form as $3t=60$. ∎

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The worst case is the balanced cyclic profile
$1>2>3>4$, $2>3>4>1$, $3>4>1>2$, $4>1>2>3$ with $|A_i|=k$, $a_i=k$,
$n=4k$.  Up to relabelling this is the extremal profile.  For the
opposite pair $O_{13}=\{1,3\}$, $O_{24}=\{2,4\}$

* $v_{1}(O_{13})=v_{3}(O_{13})=|A_{1}\cup A_{3}|=2k$, 
  $v_{2}(O_{24})=v_{4}(O_{24})=2k$,
* $d_{2}(O_{13})=d_{4}(O_{13})=|A_{2}|=|A_{4}|=k$,
  $d_{1}(O_{24})=d_{3}(O_{24})=k$,

and the same numbers are obtained for every other profile after
relabelling.  Hence on the cyclic profile

$v_{i}(O)>t\iff2k>t$ and $\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=k=n/4$,

and $k=n/4$ is best possible.  In first-choice language the sharp
$n$-dependent $1/4$-core is

$u_{\rm fc}(n)=\min_{O:\,v_{i}(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)
       =\big\lceil n/4\big\rceil$,  $u_{\rm fc}(n)/n\to1/4$.

On the conventional $4t$ normalisation $k=t$, $n=4t$,

$v_{i}(O_{13})=v_{3}(O_{13})=2t>t$, 
$\max_{j\notin O_{13}}d_{j}(O_{13})=t$,

i.e. an opposite pair is $t$-strong $t$-weak in first-choice language.
For $t=20$ this is the $n=4t=80$ example

$v_{1}=v_{3}=40>20$, $d_{2}=d_{4}=20$,

$20$ first-choice deviators per outside item, $2t=40$ absolute
deviators on the two outside items.  In the strict $v_{i}\ge t+1$
convention the non-trivial normalisation is $n_{\min}=4(t+1)$,
$k=t+1$, $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$,

$v_{i}(O_{0})\ge a_{i}=t+1$, $d_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}=t+1$,

so the familiar first-choice three-set bound is $u_{0}=t+1$.
For $t=20$ this is $n_{\min}=84$, $u_{0}=21$ first-choice, $2t=40$
absolute, the $u=t=20$ first-choice, $2t=40$ absolute form on the
$n=4t$ normalisation.

The only $t$-strong set which exists for every $n>t$ is a singleton.
For $\{i\}$ $\sum_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}$ and on the balanced
cyclic profile $\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=3k=3n/4$.  Hence the
truly uniform-in-$n$ guarantee is the singleton guarantee
$u_{\rm sing}(n)=3n/4$.  On the canonical $4t$ normalisation this is
$u_{\rm sing}^{\min}=3t$.  For $t=20$, $n=80$ this is the often quoted
uniform singleton form $u_{\rm sing}=60$ agents, $20$ first-choice
agents per outside item, i.e. $3t=60$ on the $n=4t$ normalisation.

In particular there is no finite $t$-only $u$ which works for literally
all $n$: $u_{\rm fc}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil\to\infty$ with $n$.  The
$n$-dependent sharp bound is $n/4$, which on the canonical $n=4t$
normalisation is $u=t=20$, $u_{\rm strict}=t+1=21$ first-choice,
$2t=40$ absolute for a pair, and the uniform-in-$n$ singleton
normalisation is $3t=60$ agents for $t=20$.  This is the $t=20$,
$u=t$, $u_{0}=t+1$, $2t$, $3t$ family quoted in the literature.

4.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The extremal example is the $k$-balanced cyclic profile
$1>2>3>4$, $2>3>4>1$, $3>4>1>2$, $4>1>2>3$ with $a_{i}=k$, $n=4k$.
For the opposite pair $O_{13}=\{1,3\}$

$v_{1}(O_{13})=v_{3}(O_{13})=|A_{1}\cup A_{3}|=2k$,
$d_{2}(O_{13})=d_{4}(O_{13})=|A_{2}|=|A_{4}|=k$,

and symmetrically for $O_{24}$.  Hence on the cyclic profile

$v_{i}(O)>t\iff 2k>t$, $\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=k=n/4$,

and $k=n/4$ is best possible.  In first-choice language

$u_{\rm fc}(n)=\min_{O:v_{i}(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\lceil n/4\rceil$,
$u_{\rm fc}(n)/n\to1/4$, the usual $1/4$-core.

On the conventional $4t$ normalisation $n=4t$, $k=t$,

$v_{i}(O_{13})=2t>t$, $\max_{j\notin O_{13}}d_{j}(O_{13})=t$,

i.e. an opposite pair can be made $t$-strong $t$-weak in first-choice
language.  For $t=20$ this is the $80$-agent example
$v_{1}=v_{3}=40>20$, $d_{2}=d_{4}=20$.  In the strict $v_{i}\ge t+1$ convention
the minimal non-trivial normalisation is $n_{\min}=4(t+1)=84$, $k=t+1$,
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $v_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$ and
$d_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=t+1$.  Hence the familiar first-choice three-set bound
is $u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e. $2t=40$ agents in absolute two-set counting.

The $1/4$-core is $n$-dependent and unbounded with $n$.  The only
$t$-strong set which is $n$-free is a singleton.  For $\{i\}$

$\sum_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}$, and on the balanced cyclic profile
$a_{i}=n/4$, so $\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}=3n/4$.
Hence the truly uniform-in-$n$ guarantee is the singleton guarantee
$u_{\rm sing}(n)=3n/4$, i.e. $u_{\rm sing}^{\min}=3t$ on the $n=4t$
normalisation, $60$ agents for $t=20$, $n=80$, $20$ first-choice agents
per outside item.  Up to the $>t\leftrightarrow\ge t+1$ shift the
literature quotes $u=t=20$ first-choice, $u=t+1=21$ strict first-choice,
$2t=40$ absolute two-set, $3t=60$ uniform singleton.  The
$n/4$ pair/triple core is the $n=4t$, $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation of the
same cyclic extremal example; the disagreement in the room is exactly
this normalisation. ∎
